paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Wave–particle duality is the idea in quantum mechanics that basic entities such as photons and electrons show wave properties or particle properties, depending on the experiment. It reflects the fact that the classical notions of a particle and of a wave cannot, by themselves, fully describe how quantum objects behave. The word duality was chosen to name these seeming contradictions.

paragraphs.heading: Two classical models
paragraphs.text: Waves and particles are two very different models, and each covers a huge range of things. A classical wave has values at many points in space that change over time, its spread can change through diffraction, and it shows interference; water waves, sound and radio waves are examples. A classical particle has a center of mass and a size, and follows a path set by its changing position and velocity, which is a straight line when no forces act. Particle models work for stars, planets, tennis balls and sand grains alike. Unlike waves, particles do not interfere.

paragraphs.heading: Light, from wave to particle
paragraphs.text: In the late 1600s Isaac Newton held that light was made of particles, while Christiaan Huygens described it as a wave. The wave model was backed by Thomas Young's interference experiments of 1801 and by François Arago, who detected the Poisson spot in 1819. Then in 1901 Max Planck's law for black-body radiation assumed that a hypothetical charged oscillator could only change its energy in minimal steps proportional to frequency. In 1905 Albert Einstein explained the photoelectric effect with discrete photon energies, and both results pointed to particle behavior.

paragraphs.heading: Momentum seals it
paragraphs.text: The photon theory stayed controversial even after several experiments supported it. Arthur Compton's experiments from 1922 to 1924, which showed that light carries momentum, finally settled the matter. This evidence of particle-like energy and momentum seemed to clash with the older experiments showing light interfering like a wave.

paragraphs.heading: Electrons, from particle to wave
paragraphs.text: For electrons the evidence came in the opposite order: first particles, then waves. After de Broglie proposed that electrons also have a wave side, Erwin Schrödinger developed a wave equation for electrons in 1925 to 1926. In 1926 Max Born spoke at an Oxford meeting about using electron diffraction to confirm the idea, citing data from Clinton Davisson, who happened to be in the room. Davisson returned to his lab in the US and switched his focus to testing the wave property of electrons. In 1927 two experiments confirmed it: Davisson and Germer at Bell Labs scattered electrons off nickel surfaces, and George Paget Thomson and Alexander Reid at Cambridge sent electrons through thin nickel films and saw rings of diffraction.

paragraphs.heading: Not just electrons
paragraphs.text: Davisson and Thomson received the Nobel Prize in 1937 for showing the wave properties of electrons through diffraction. In the 1930s Otto Stern ran similar crystal diffraction experiments with beams of helium atoms and hydrogen molecules. These showed that wave behavior is not limited to electrons but is a general property of matter.

paragraphs.heading: How the two fit together
paragraphs.text: In quantum systems, some experiments show wave-like interference and diffraction, while others show particle-like collisions. The theory uses wave equations that predict how particles are likely to be spread out. The chance of detecting a particle at a given point is the square of a wave whose values are complex numbers. Particles arrive one at a time and at random, yet together they build up a pattern, so large numbers of random hits can display wave-like behavior.
